pm2-who-should-work.reason: Teaches span of control, RACI and character-first selection, but never plainly says what Jethro saw (one man carrying what should be shared) or why that stalls a team.
pm2-who-should-work.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What did Jethro see in Moses? A leader carrying the whole load alone. His remedy was not to work harder but to share the burden: set able people in tiers, choose them first for character, and bring only the great matters up. As Jethro put it, "so shall it be easier for thyself, and they shall bear the burden with thee." Here is how that settles who should work.
pm2-who-should-work.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your team stalls when everything waits on you, and Jethro saw that in Moses. The fix he gave is still the fix: place able people, chosen for character before skill, men of truth who hate covetousness (Exodus 18:21), give them real lanes, and let the burden become shared rather than offloaded. And no lane is a lesser seat, because Yahweh set every member in the body as it pleased Him (1 Corinthians 12:18). Step out of everyone's job, and the work moves.

teen.open: Jethro saw Moses trying to do everything himself. His advice was simple: share the load with honest, able people.
teen.close: So if your group is stuck, maybe you are holding too much. Pick trustworthy people, give them real jobs, and let them carry it with you.

senior.open: Jethro watched his son-in-law carry the whole people alone, and named the problem. The answer he gave Moses is the answer for a stalled team today.
senior.close: So the lesson lands where Jethro did. A team moves when the leader shares the burden with able people of proven character, in clear lanes, and keeps only the great matters for himself.

pm1-count-the-cost.reason: The one question (whether he have sufficient to finish it) appears mid-lesson after industry framing; it is never stated as the plain answer to "can you finish?" and the end leans on comparison with standards.
pm1-count-the-cost.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What is the one question Yahweh asks before you say yes to a project? Whether you have enough to finish it. Not enough to start, not enough for the first phase, but enough to see it through, checked before the foundation is laid (Luke 14:28). Here is why the Word is stricter than an estimate.
pm1-count-the-cost.example: A SLAB AND NO WALLS. Say a congregation needs $400,000 for a new hall and has $150,000 in hand. Saying yes on the strength of the first phase pours a slab. Then the money runs out, and for three years the people who gave walk past a slab on the way into church. Asking the finish question first would have meant preparing the field (Proverbs 24:27): raising or planning the whole before breaking ground.
pm1-count-the-cost.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you finish what you start? The Word says find out before you say yes. Sit down and count whether you have sufficient to finish it, the whole job and not one phase. Prepare the field first, then build the house (Proverbs 24:27), and do not let haste rush the gate, because haste leads to want (Proverbs 21:5). Count the finish first, and you protect both the money and the trust of the people who gave.

teen.open: Before you start anything big, Yahweh's Word asks one question: do you have enough to finish it?
teen.close: So count the whole cost first, not just the start. Finishing well keeps people's trust.

senior.open: The Word asks a single question before any project begins: is there sufficient to finish it? This lesson shows why that question comes before the plan.
senior.close: So the answer is to count the whole cost before committing. Sufficiency to finish, judged before the foundation, guards the giving and the credibility of those who trusted you with it.

pm3-the-skill-is-given-and-named.reason: Bezaleel is never named in the text; the answer (Yahweh names and fills the craftsman, names a second lead, and gives the gift to teach) is scattered across industry vocabulary.
pm3-the-skill-is-given-and-named.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who gets named for the hard build? In Exodus 31 Yahweh names a craftsman, Bezaleel, and fills him with wisdom, understanding and knowledge for real trade work. He also names a second lead, and He puts teaching inside the gift (Exodus 35:34). The person named is the skilled builder who can pass the skill on. Here is what that means for your project.
pm3-the-skill-is-given-and-named.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. The one named for the hard build is the craftsman Yahweh filled for the work, listed by real skills like gold, stone and timber, never ranked below the platform. And he is not named alone: there is a second lead, and the gift includes the heart to teach. So staff your project by capability, not headcount, and make sure no skill lives in one person. Teach it on purpose, down the chain (2 Timothy 2:2).

teen.open: For the big building job, Yahweh named a skilled worker, filled him with wisdom, and gave him the gift to teach others.
teen.close: So skilled hands matter to Yahweh. If you know how to do something, teach someone else, so the work never depends on just you.

senior.open: Exodus 31 answers this by name. Yahweh called Bezaleel, filled him for the craft, gave him a partner, and gave him the ability to teach.
senior.close: So the answer is clear. The hard build is entrusted to filled, skilled people named by their abilities, and the skill is meant to be taught onward rather than held by one person alone.

pm5-timeline-and-milestones.reason: Teaches baselines, binary milestones and Nehemiah 6:15, but never says plainly whether a project can be finished and unmeasured, or what makes a milestone real.
pm5-timeline-and-milestones.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can a project be finished and still be unmeasured? Yes, if no one wrote down the plan and the actual, or if the milestones were only phases of effort. A real milestone is done or not done, with a test for done. Nehemiah's wall carries both its date and its fifty-two days, and the hard days too (Nehemiah 6:15). Here is how that record works.
pm5-timeline-and-milestones.example: SEVENTY PERCENT FOR FOUR MONTHS. Say a milestone reads: electrical in progress. Every week it reports seventy percent, because effort keeps going in. Now rewrite it as: panel installed and passed inspection. That is either true or not. The first can stay at seventy percent for four months. The second tells you on the day it is done, and the gap between the planned date and the real one is right there to see.
pm5-timeline-and-milestones.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. A project can be finished and unmeasured when it never had a dated plan or honest checkpoints. Nehemiah's wall is the opposite: the date, the duration, and the interruptions are all in the record. So set milestones you can check as done or not done, know the state of your work diligently as a duty of stewardship (Proverbs 27:23), and hold the schedule firmly enough to measure but with room for each season's purpose (Ecclesiastes 3:1).

teen.open: Yes, you can finish something and never really know how it went. Real milestones are clear: done or not done, with a date.
teen.close: So write down the plan and what actually happened, like Nehemiah's wall with its fifty-two days. Then you know, instead of guessing.

senior.open: A project can reach its end without anyone being able to say how it went against the plan. The dated wall of Nehemiah shows the remedy.
senior.close: So the answer is to record both the plan and the actual, as Nehemiah 6:15 does, with milestones that are plainly complete or not. Knowing the true state is part of faithful stewardship.

pm4-what-we-do-not-need-to-do.reason: Names scope creep early, but never ties it plainly to why hard-working teams still run late; the scope question itself is stated only in the final sentence.
pm4-what-we-do-not-need-to-do.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why do projects run late when everyone works hard? Because work keeps entering without a decision, often as a favour or a good idea from someone with standing. The effort is real, but it goes to things that do not belong to the finish line. Nehemiah's question before every detour was whether it belonged to the work at all, and his answer was often no (Nehemiah 6:3).
pm4-what-we-do-not-need-to-do.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Projects run late with everyone working hard because hard work is spent on what was never decided. The cure is the question Nehemiah kept asking: does this belong to the finish line? If not, the answer is no, and you need not argue the idea on its merits, because arguing is itself the interruption. Only one thing is needful (Luke 10:42), and searching out the root of a matter is honourable work (Proverbs 25:2). Say no well, and the wall gets finished.

teen.open: Projects run late when extra jobs sneak in. Everyone is busy, but on things that were never part of the plan.
teen.close: So ask Nehemiah's question: does this help finish the work? If not, it is okay to say no.

senior.open: Hard work does not keep a project on time if the work keeps growing without a decision. Nehemiah faced exactly that, and answered it plainly.
senior.close: So the reason is scope that enters unchecked, and the remedy is the first question: does this belong to the finish? A plain, unargued no is a normal and rightful answer.

pm7-the-watchman-and-the-risk.reason: States early that the watchman is held responsible for silence, but ends on Proverbs 13:16 as disposition rather than landing who owns the unmentioned problem.
pm7-the-watchman-and-the-risk.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who is responsible for the problem nobody mentioned? The one who was posted to watch for it. In Ezekiel 33:6 the watchman who sees the danger and stays silent carries the blame. So every real risk needs a named owner and a clear signal that it is arriving. Here is how the watch works.
pm7-the-watchman-and-the-risk.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. The problem nobody mentioned belongs to the watchman who saw it and kept quiet. So give every risk an owner and a trigger, keep the watch continuous like Nehemiah's, day and night (Nehemiah 4:9), and make the trumpet welcome in your house, because raising the alarm is loyalty, not disloyalty. Pray and set the watch, both. Prudence acts on what it knows (Proverbs 13:16). Name the watchman, and the silence has someone to break it.

teen.open: If you see a problem coming and say nothing, part of it is on you. That is the watchman's job in the Bible.
teen.close: So speak up when you see trouble coming. Saying it out loud is loyal, not rude.

senior.close: So the answer is the watchman. Whoever is set to watch and sees the danger is accountable to sound the alarm, and a wise house names that person and welcomes the trumpet.

pm6-the-counsellors-you-secure.reason: The answer (bring one bounded question and leave with a fact, a number or a named constraint, from someone who does the trade) appears mid-lesson; it ends on pricing from memory.
pm6-the-counsellors-you-secure.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What should you ask the expert before your next build? One bounded question that helps you see: something that sends you away with a fact, a number, or a named limit. You are not there to get your plan approved. You are there to get sight, from someone who actually does the work, before you price it. Here is why the Word puts counsel first.
pm6-the-counsellors-you-secure.example: ONE QUESTION, ONE NUMBER. Say your rehab budget has a line for the roof that you priced from memory. Instead of asking a roofer whether your plan looks good, you ask one bounded question: what will this roof need, and what will it cost? You leave with a number and a named constraint. The first meeting would have given you a nod. The second gives you a budget line you can stand on.
pm6-the-counsellors-you-secure.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Before your next build, ask the expert one bounded question that gives you sight, not approval, and walk out with a fact, a number, or a named constraint. Counsel does not just make a plan look better; it is how the purpose is established. Answering before hearing is folly and shame (Proverbs 18:13). So price no trade from memory. Ask the one who does it, and guessing stops being expensive.

teen.open: Before you build or plan something, ask someone who really knows. Ask one clear question and come away with a real answer.
teen.close: So do not guess. Ask the person who does the work, listen first, and then plan.

senior.open: The lesson answers this practically: go to someone who does the work, with one bounded question, and come away seeing clearly.
senior.close: So the question to bring is the one that yields a fact, a number, or a named constraint. That kind of counsel establishes a plan, while answering before hearing only adds cost and shame.

pm9-the-change-you-put-down.reason: The answer (no: continuing must be re-justified on today's facts, and stopping rightly is success) is present but wrapped in sunk-cost and stage-gate jargon and never said as a plain no.
pm9-the-change-you-put-down.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Should you keep going just because you already paid? No. Money and effort already spent are a sunk cost: they are gone whether you go on or stop. Whether to continue must be decided on what is true now, not on what was spent. And a project stopped for the right reason is a success, not a disgrace. Here is the posture that makes that possible.
pm9-the-change-you-put-down.example: THE CHAMPION AT THE GATE. Say a ministry has spent two years on a building plan its leader first proposed. At the scheduled review, current facts say the plan no longer fits. The money spent cannot come back either way. The only real question is whether the next dollar and the next month are justified today. The hardest part is that the leader who started it must be humble enough to say stop.
pm9-the-change-you-put-down.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. No, what you already paid is not a reason to keep going. Set a planned point to reconsider, and re-justify the project there on current facts. Forget what lies behind and reach forward like Paul, who acted without claiming to have arrived (Philippians 3:13), and do not keep looking back once your hand is on the plough (Luke 9:62). It takes humility, because the one who must recommend stopping is often the one who started. Record a right stop as a success, and your people will be free to stop when they should.

teen.open: Should you keep going just because you already spent a lot? No. What is spent is gone either way.
teen.close: So decide based on what is true now. Stopping for a good reason is not failing. It takes humility, and it is a win.

senior.open: The title raises the sunk-cost question, and the lesson answers it: what has been spent is not, by itself, a reason to continue.
senior.close: So the answer is no. Each continuation must stand on present facts, and a project stopped for the right reason should be recorded as a success. That takes the humility to be wrong.

pm8-the-plumbline.reason: The answer (done must be checked against a standard written before the work, outside the builder, applied equally to all) is implied through the plumbline image; it never says plainly what makes done checkable.
pm8-the-plumbline.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your project's finish something anyone could check? It should be. A real standard is written before the work starts, sits outside the builder like a plumbline, and reports true or not true no matter how hard anyone worked. An opinion changes with the person; a standard does not. Here is how Yahweh's plumbline teaches it.
pm8-the-plumbline.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your project's finish is checkable when it is measured against a standard set before the work, held outside the builder, and indifferent to effort, as Yahweh's plumbline is (Amos 7:7-8). Check it during the work, not only at the end, and do not despise the small parts (Zechariah 4:10). And use one standard for everyone: the contractor, the volunteers, and yourself. Two weights is a false balance (Proverbs 11:1). One standard anyone could check is what makes done mean done.

teen.open: Done should mean something anyone could check, not just someone's opinion. Yahweh's plumbline shows how.
teen.close: So agree on what done looks like before you start, check as you go, and use the same rule for everyone, including yourself.

senior.open: An opinion is not a standard. The lesson asks whether our idea of done could be checked by anyone, and the plumbline in Amos gives the measure.
senior.close: So done is honest when a standard written in advance, outside the builder and blind to effort, is applied the same way to every worker, our own included. Anything else is a false balance.

pm11-how-the-organization-learns-priorit.reason: Diagnoses information overload early but the how (shared system, taught standard, tiers, escalation, reading the times, written plain, counsel, inspection) is scattered across cases; ends on whose standard.
pm11-how-the-organization-learns-priorit.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How would you spot the pattern before it costs you? Do not keep it all in one head. Build a system that sees: a taught standard, able people in tiers, a rule for what comes up to you, the vision written plain, and many counsellors. Then let Yahweh inspect it, in numbers and in fruit. Here is how the Word shows it, case by case.
pm11-how-the-organization-learns-priorit.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. You spot the pattern by refusing to let it live in one memory. Teach the standard, place qualified people, set the escalation rule (Exodus 18:20-22). Read the times and know what to do, as Issachar did (1 Chronicles 12:32), and turn what you see into a repeatable system, as Joseph did (Genesis 41:34). Look before you build, write it plain, take many counsellors. Then consider your ways honestly (Haggai 1:5). An organization that can see, decide and be inspected can do His will before the cost arrives.

teen.open: When there is too much information, the answer is not a smarter boss. It is a team that shares what it sees.
teen.close: So write things down, share the load, ask for advice, and check your ways honestly. Then you see the problem before it hurts.

senior.open: The lesson begins with a plain diagnosis: leaders drown in information, not tasks. The Word answers with governance that does not depend on one person.
senior.close: So the pattern is spotted by a system, not a single memory: a taught standard, qualified people, an escalation rule, a plain written vision, and many counsellors, all open to Yahweh's inspection.

pm10-the-record-that-outlives-it.reason: The answer (closeout: an honest record, plain writing others can run with, people taught to carry it on) is spread through industry terms; it ends on faithfulness, not on what lasts.
pm10-the-record-that-outlives-it.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If the project is not finished when the building is, what is left? The closeout: a record of what was built and who carries it, written plain enough that someone else can run with it, and people taught to keep it going after you. Nehemiah finished the wall and then made the register (Nehemiah 7:5). Here is how to leave something that lasts.
pm10-the-record-that-outlives-it.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your project is finished when what you built can keep working without you. That takes three things: the register, like Nehemiah's after the wall; a plain record another reader can run on (Habakkuk 2:2); and people taught to teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). This is the part nobody watches, which is exactly where faithfulness shows (Luke 16:10). Close it out well, and the work lasts longer than the builder.

teen.open: A project is not really done when it is built. It is done when someone else can keep it going.
teen.close: So write it down clearly, teach others how it works, and finish the part nobody sees. That is what lasts.

senior.open: Many projects stop at the visible result. Nehemiah and Habakkuk show that the work is not complete until it is recorded, made usable, and handed on.
senior.close: So the building is not the end. A plain record, a proper handover, and people taught to carry the work forward are what make it last, and faithfulness in that quiet part is what Yahweh sees.

pm12-titles-and-fruits-capability-shown-.reason: The thesis (titles screen potential, outcomes show capability) is stated early, but it never says plainly whether a title is a ceiling; ownership arrives in section five.
pm12-titles-and-fruits-capability-shown-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your title your ceiling? No. A title may limit how others see you, but it does not limit what you can do. Capability is shown in outcomes, the way David answered Saul with his record of the lion and the bear, and gave Yahweh the credit (1 Samuel 17:34-37). Recognition may come late, or not at all, but ownership does not have to wait.
pm12-titles-and-fruits-capability-shown-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your title is not your ceiling. Committees read titles because titles are easy to check, but Yahweh looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7), and people are known by their fruit (Matthew 7:16). Joseph was given charge before he had rank. So keep owning the work, faithful in the very little (Luke 16:10), and present your outcomes as evidence others can confirm, with Yahweh credited for them. Even if no one remembers, wisdom is still better than strength.

teen.open: Your title does not set your limit. What you actually do shows who you are, like David and his lion and bear.
teen.close: So keep doing good work, give Yahweh the credit, and let your results speak. The title might come later, or not, but your growth does not wait for it.

senior.open: Many have carried real responsibility without the title that goes with it. The lesson asks whether that title is the limit, and answers from David and Joseph.
senior.close: So the title is not the ceiling. Capability is shown in outcomes, credited to Yahweh and confirmed by others, and the ownership that does not wait for recognition is itself the proof.

pm13-selected-designed-procured-built-an.reason: The answer (tools change the how, Yahweh establishes the house) arrives only in section three after a long source audit; the lesson ends on talk-it-over practices.
pm13-selected-designed-procured-built-an.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who establishes the house when the tools change? Yahweh does. Digital and A.I. tools can change how a project is selected, designed, procured, built and steered, but they cannot change Who establishes the work. The house stands "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). Here is how to count the cost and steer under Him.
pm13-selected-designed-procured-built-an.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. When the tools change, the One who establishes the house does not. New tools are only the how. Count whether you have sufficient to finish before you lay the foundation (Luke 14:28). Build on the only foundation, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), and commit your works to the LORD so your thoughts are established (Proverbs 16:3). Challenge an at-risk project with many counsellors instead of coddling it, raise taught people, and steer by a plumbline held from outside the work. Yahweh establishes; we steward faithfully.

teen.open: New tools like A.I. change how we build things. They do not change Who makes the work stand. Yahweh does.
teen.close: So use the tools, but count the cost first, get honest advice, and build on Jesus. Yahweh is the One who makes it last.

senior.open: Tools for capital projects change from one generation to the next. This lesson asks who establishes the house through all of it, and answers from Zechariah and Luke.
senior.close: So the answer stands. Tools change the method, but Yahweh establishes the house. Our part is to count the cost to finish, build on Christ, accept honest counsel, and steer by a standard outside ourselves.

pm14-whose-measure-the-benchmark-the-cen.reason: The test (who is selling it, is there a sample and a definition) is buried in a long source audit; the Word's replacement measure comes later and the lesson ends on family practice.
pm14-whose-measure-the-benchmark-the-cen.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How would you know if a growth number measures anything? Ask who is selling it, what it counted, and how it defined what it counted. "A benchmark without its sample and its definition is not a fact." And then measure by Yahweh's rule for your own assignment, not by comparing yourself with others (2 Corinthians 10:12-13). Here is the audit, and the measures the Word already gave us.
pm14-whose-measure-the-benchmark-the-cen.example: THE NUMBER THAT MOVED. The email in this lesson sold a benchmark against 76M subscribers in its preheader, and said 75 million in its body, in the same message. Neither said what a subscriber was. A search turned up earlier, lower figures from the same vendor, unconfirmed. And the count was drawn from the vendor's own customers. Once checked, the solid-sounding number became a moving claim with no definition and a seller behind it.
pm14-whose-measure-the-benchmark-the-cen.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. You know a number measures something when it has a source, a sample and a definition you can see, and when it serves your assignment rather than your pride. Counting is not the sin; David's census was, because he wanted his own strength. So drop the sold benchmark and keep the Word's measures: fruit, daily occasions, faithfulness, your own work proved, praise from others, an honest ledger, and sufficiency to finish. Measured that way, the increase is credited where it belongs, to Yahweh.

teen.open: If a number comes with a sales pitch, ask who counted it and what they counted. If you cannot tell, it is not a fact.
teen.close: So check the source before you trust a number. Then measure yourself by Yahweh's standard, not by comparing yourself to everyone else.

senior.open: A growth figure sold with an offer deserves a question before it earns trust. The lesson shows how to ask it, and what measure to use instead.
senior.close: So a number earns trust only when its sample and definition are open to view. Beyond that, the Word gives its own measures, and the increase is Yahweh's gift rather than our own strength.

pm15-sat-where-they-sat-the-oldest-forwa.reason: Opens on the email source; the answer (nearness first, then the word; necessary but not sufficient; counsel from one whose sheep they are) emerges across the cases and ends on family practice.
pm15-sat-where-they-sat-the-oldest-forwa.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Before you give advice, have you sat where they sat? The Word sets the order: be near first, speak second. Ezekiel sat among the captives seven days before he spoke (Ezekiel 3:15), Nehemiah looked at the broken walls himself, and Jethro watched a whole day and began with a question. Nearness is needed, but it is not enough; the counsel must also be right, and given by someone with a stake.
pm15-sat-where-they-sat-the-oldest-forwa.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Have you sat where they sat? That is the first thing the Word asks of anyone who would advise. Ezekiel sat, Nehemiah looked, and Jethro watched before they spoke, and Paul worked the same craft beside the people he taught. But nearness is not the whole of it: Job's friends sat well and spoke wrongly. So listen before you answer (Proverbs 18:13), care like a shepherd and not a hireling (John 10:12-13), and follow Jesus, who came and dwelt among us.

teen.open: Before you tell someone what to do, spend time where they are and see what they see. That is how the Bible does it.
teen.close: So sit with people first, listen all the way, then speak like someone who cares. Being there matters, and so does saying what is true.

senior.open: The Word has an old pattern for anyone who would counsel others: be present first. Ezekiel, Nehemiah and Jethro each show it.
senior.close: So the answer is that advice must follow nearness. Sit where they sat, see the breaks yourself, listen before answering, and speak as one who carries the burden with them, after the way of Jesus, who came near.

pm16-divers-weights-in-the-bag.reason: Opens on the forwarded ad and the unread report; the answer (one perfect and just weight through every door, Deut 25:13-15) arrives mid-lesson and it ends on a family talk, not the answer.
pm16-divers-weights-in-the-bag.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your business still the same business through every door a customer walks through? Only if one measure travels with you everywhere: the same price, the same promise, the same terms, the same character, whether someone meets you in the app, on the phone or at the counter. Two weights in one bag, one for here and one for there, is what the Word forbids (Deuteronomy 25:13-15). Here is how the Word shows it, and how this house caught itself.
pm16-divers-weights-in-the-bag.example: ONE PRICE, TWO DOORS. Say a small shop lists a repair at $80 on its website, and the person answering the phone quotes $95 because the website was never updated. Nobody meant to keep two prices. But a customer who sees the site and then calls has now met two businesses. The fix is not a corrected second price list. It is one price written down in one place, with the phone script and the website both reading from it, so they cannot drift apart again.
pm16-divers-weights-in-the-bag.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your business still the same business through every door? It is when a person who meets you twice finds the same weight both times. The Word calls two measures an abomination and calls the just weight His delight (Proverbs 11:1). Divers weights rarely arrive by decision; they pile up one convenient change at a time. So count every door, write the one message in one place, walk through each door as a stranger would, and make the places that must agree read from one source. Then you are one business, and the promise holds: length of days.

teen.open: The title asks if a business stays the same business no matter where you meet it. It should. Same price, same promise, same character, in the app, on the phone, or in person.
teen.close: So, is it the same business through every door? Only when it keeps one weight, not two. Yahweh delights in a just weight, and people trust what stays the same.

senior.open: The title asks whether a business remains the same business through every door a customer uses. The Word's answer is that it must carry one perfect and just measure everywhere, not a great one in one place and a small one in another.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. A business is the same through every door when the price, the promise and the character match wherever a person meets it, and the Word ties that just weight to length of days.

pm17-can-two-walk-together.reason: After a long provenance preamble, Amos 3:3 states the answer, but it is spread over nine movements and the lesson ends on a family talk and fruit verses, not on agreeing before spending.
pm17-can-two-walk-together.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does Yahweh's Word teach about agreeing before you spend? That the agreement comes first, not last: two cannot walk together except they be agreed (Amos 3:3). The one who buys and the one who counts are both honoured by name, both put their hands on the count where money moves, and then trust the faithful people past that gate. And all of it is His money. Here is how the Word shows it.
pm17-can-two-walk-together.example: TWO NAMES, ONE PURCHASE. Say a household is about to buy a $1,200 appliance. One spouse found it and wants it; the other keeps the budget. Before anything is ordered, they sit down together, agree on the one number that matters (what the budget can carry this month), and both look at the account at the same time, the way the king's scribe and the high priest came up together to the chest (2 Kings 12:10). Once they agree, the buyer goes and buys without being second-guessed at every step.
pm17-can-two-walk-together.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does Yahweh's Word teach about agreeing before you spend? Agree first, because walking together comes after the agreement (Amos 3:3). Name both offices, as Exodus 38 names Bezaleel who made and Ithamar who counted. Put two hands on the count at the gate, then trust faithful hands past it (2 Kings 12:15). Keep it honest in the sight of men as well as the Lord (2 Corinthians 8:21), look for pride before you blame the process, and remember whose silver it is. Then the two offices walk together, and the money arrives where it was sent.

teen.open: The title asks what the Word says about agreeing before you spend. Simple answer: agree first. Two cannot walk together unless they are agreed (Amos 3:3).
teen.close: So agree before you spend. Let the one who buys and the one who counts look at it together, then trust each other. It is Yahweh's money, and both jobs matter.

senior.open: The title asks what Yahweh's Word teaches about agreeing before money is spent. Its answer is that agreement comes first, and that the one who buys and the one who keeps the record each hold an honoured office.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Agree first, set two hands on the count where money moves, trust faithful people beyond that point, and keep the books honest in the sight of men as well as the Lord, because the silver is His.

pm18-what-is-that-in-thine-hand.reason: The answer (start with what is in the hand, show the way, spend time beside them, and Yahweh teaches the mouth) is spread across seven movements after a long source note; ends on family talk.
pm18-what-is-that-in-thine-hand.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does Moses' rod teach leaders about capability anxiety, the fear that your skills will not keep up? Begin where Yahweh began: What is that in thine hand? (Exodus 4:2). Name what your people can already do, show them the way and the work ahead (Exodus 18:20), and spend real time beside them. Then point them to the Teacher who promised, I will be with thy mouth (Exodus 4:12). Here is how the Word shows it.
pm18-what-is-that-in-thine-hand.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does Moses' rod teach a leader about a worried team? That your people already hold something, and the work starts there. Yahweh asked about the rod before He gave the commission, and the old shepherd's stick went into the new work. He answered fear with a promise and a plan, not contempt. So take inventory of what is in their hands, show them the way and the work, be with them before you send them, and remind them that sufficiency comes from Yahweh, who makes able and still teaches the mouth.

teen.open: The title asks what Moses' rod teaches about feeling like you cannot keep up. Yahweh started with what Moses already had in his hand, not with what he lacked.
teen.close: So start with what is already in your hand. Yahweh used a plain stick, taught Moses what to say, and stayed with him. He does the same with you.

senior.open: The title asks what Moses' rod teaches leaders about people who fear their skills will not keep up. Yahweh began with an inventory, What is that in thine hand, and then promised to be with Moses' mouth and teach him.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. A good leader starts with what people already hold, shows them the way and the work, and spends time beside them, while every worker rests on the One who makes us able and does not change.

pm19-let-these-also-first-be-proved.reason: The answer (first be proved, then the office; weigh the letter, the report of those who watched, and the trial) is spread across eight movements and the lesson ends on family talk, not on the question.
pm19-let-these-also-first-be-proved.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Your résumé says yes, but who has watched you work? That is the question the Word asks too: let these also first be proved, then the office (1 Timothy 3:10). Daniel asked for a short trial, Apollos carried a letter and kept learning, and Timothy had people who watched him serve. Readiness is shown in real work, weighed by every honest signal together. Here is how the Word shows it.
pm19-let-these-also-first-be-proved.example: TEN DAYS INSTEAD OF A PAGE. Say a small church needs a new treasurer, and one candidate has a polished résumé. Following Daniel's pattern, the board asks for a short, real trial: keep the books for one month beside the current treasurer. They also read the reference letter and ask the people who have served with the candidate. At the end, they decide on the letter, the report and the work together, and not on the page alone.
pm19-let-these-also-first-be-proved.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your résumé says yes, but who has watched you work? The Word wants that answered before the office is given. Daniel was proved ten days and examined in person. Apollos carried a letter and kept learning from Aquila and Priscilla. Timothy was proved serving beside Paul, and the strongest word about him came from the one who watched. So ask for the work, weigh the letter, the report and the trial together, and give the young a place to use their judgment. We prove our work; grace alone settles our worth.

teen.open: The title asks who has actually watched you work. A paper can say you are ready, but the Word says to be proved first, then given the job (1 Timothy 3:10).
teen.close: So let your work show it. Daniel was tested, Timothy was watched serving. Show what you can do, and remember your worth comes from Yahweh's grace, not your work.

senior.open: The title asks a fair question about readiness: who has watched you work? The Word sets the order plainly. Let a person first be proved, and then let him hold the office.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Readiness is shown in real work and weighed by the letter, the report of those who watched, and a fair trial together, while our standing before Yahweh rests on grace, not on proof.
